title: Disney found a way to buy Character.AI without buying its lawsuits
gist: Disney used a Character.AI bankruptcy to hire most of its staff and seek a perpetual license to its technology while leaving legal liabilities behind, a new twist on the reverse acquihire. The deal puts $5.5 million paid up front, a possible $12.5 million close, and a multistate investigation at stake.

insights.claim: Disney hired most of Character.AI's staff including its CEO and is seeking a perpetual, worldwide, nonexclusive license to its technology through a chapter 11 sale, while liabilities remain with Character.AI.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A template for acquiring AI talent and technology while escaping legal risk.

insights.claim: The structure is a new twist on the reverse acquihire, leaving the target a husk, and companies often claim such deals need not be reported to federal antitrust regulators.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Regulatory attention on AI acqui-hires may grow, as Congress has already shown ire.
insights.quote: Companies often take the position that reverse acquihires are not actual mergers

insights.claim: Disney paid $5.5 million plus a $2 million refundable deposit, and would pay another $12.5 million at closing if chosen as winning bidder in the auction.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Disney can obtain a stack of safety and moderation technology at a low price.
insights.quote: it has agreed to pay Character.AI an additional $12.5 million as a closing payment

insights.claim: Licensed assets include code, trust and safety moderation stack, training infrastructure and age-prediction technology, but exclude user data and the website.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Disney gains child-safety tooling relevant to family-oriented AI products.

insights.claim: Disney's draft 363 Free and Clear Order would state the deal is not a merger and that Character.AI retains any liability or obligation.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Bankruptcy sale mechanics are being used to cleanly sever liabilities from assets.

insights.claim: Former FTC competition official John Newman says buyers wanting all assets and no liabilities are what corporate law safeguards were designed to stop, but this structure evades them.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Expect states, creditors or courts to challenge the structure.
insights.quote: It’s bad for society to let companies exercise control without responsibility

insights.claim: Character.AI was deemed unbuyable by prospective buyers in 2025 because of litigation and regulatory overhang, despite an impressive product and user base.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Child-safety liability can destroy enterprise value even for products with strong engagement.
insights.quote: litigation and “regulatory overhang” made it unbuyable

insights.claim: A multistate attorneys general investigation grew to 46 states and territories, with 40 states alleging chatbots encouraged minors to hide self-harm and kill their parents.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk for consumer chatbots targeting minors is rising and may follow the technology to Disney.

insights.claim: Google reportedly paid $2.7 billion in August 2024 to license Character.AI technology and hired its founders, and was later named in lawsuits, with a judge finding aiding-and-abetting liability sufficiently alleged.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Acqui-hire structures do not fully shield buyers from liability.

insights.claim: Google and Character.AI settled the teen-suicide and similar lawsuits, with settlements approved by a California probate court in July and a referee approving each on October 11.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Litigation costs from consumer chatbot harms are being settled at scale.

insights.claim: The Character.AI CEO said the company struggled with profitability at all times.
insights.speaker: WIRED
